newsitem.title: BURMA: Deadly bombing stuns Rangoon, Burma government.
newsitem.headline: Deadly bombing stuns Rangoon, Burma government.

text.p: Residents in Burma's capital reacted with shock and fear on Tuesday to news that a bomb had exploded at the home of one of the country's top generals, killing his daughter.
Officials from the military government said they were investigating the explosion, believed to be from a parcel bomb.
They said the government has not laid blame for the attack, while student exile groups and the rebel Karen National Union (KNU) have denied any involvement.
State-run media announced late on Monday that a bomb had exploded at the house of Lieutenant-General Tin Oo the previous evening, killing his 34-year-old daughter, Cho Lei Oo.
The official announcement said the attack was a "terrorist bomb explosion", but did not say who might be suspected.
The funeral for Cho Lei Oo, a mother of two and Tin Oo's eldest daughter, was due to be held on Tuesday afternoon.
In Rangoon, residents expressed fear after hearing the news on the official radio and television.

"I never imagined that our country would be so unsafe," said one old man after hearing about the attack in a city where news is often spread faster by word of mouth than through the tightly controlled, state-run media.
Others said they were worried about their own safety.
The attack comes on the heels of nationwide religious unrest and about 3-1/2 months after another deadly explosion at a Buddhist shrine in the outskirts of Rangoon on December 25.
The military government blamed the Karen National Union (KNU) ethnic guerrilla group for that attack, in which two bombs exploded, killing five people and wounding 17.

Tin Oo, one of the four most powerful members of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), was the last senior official to visit the sacred Tooth Relic Pagoda before the explosion on Christmas Day.
He is one of the hardliners in the SLORC, and often gives speeches urging troops and citizens to "annihilate" anyone who tries to disturb the stability of the state.

Some diplomats said Tin Oo, who is army chief of staff and whose government title is Secretary Two of the SLORC, might have been injured in the Sunday night attack. Others said they had heard he was not hurt.
But many residents noticed he did not appear on television on Monday night at the ceremonies he usually attended.

Security continued to be tight in Rangoon, especially near Tin Oo's house in an elite residential neighbourhood and around the Number Two Military Hospital, where Cho Lei Oo apparently had been taken.
Military officials told Reuters that security had also been increased around the homes of other top SLORC members.
Troops and tanks have been deployed throughout the city since December, when students staged a series of rare street demonstrations against the military government.
In mid-March, religious troubles broke out between Buddhist monks and Moslems, and the government issued a curfew and restrictions in some parts of the country.

The government also sent hundreds of extra troops to patrol the streets before the March 27 Armed Forces Day. Authorities said officials feared a terrorist attack around that day, when all top military brass would be in Rangoon.
